Square-Body Chevy Silverado Sat 15 Years Untouched, Rescuers Have 72 Hours To Make It Great Again
61 photos
Photo: YouTube/WD Detailing
What would you do, and how would you feel knowing you have 72 hours to complete a task that just landed in your lap, under the threat of losing your job right before Thanksgiving? (Talk about completely F-ing up the timing. F is for Friday, by the way. Which is today, because that's when the deadline expires).
That high-stakes ultimatum hit Adam, WD Detailing’s trusty mechanic, who got the scare straight from RJ while contemplating a Rounded Line square-body. The 1987 Chevrolet R20 Silverado regular-cab long-bed was dragged out of a remote barn after 15 years of neglect. Somehow, pickup truck years put against car years seem to be the equivalent of dog years compared to human years. for every years that passes over a passenger car, it looks like seven have trampled over the humble utilitarian.
Flat tires carved deep trenches across the dirt floor during extraction. The crew's mission was brutal: detail the heavy-duty hauler spotless and make it start, idle, drive, and stop within 72 hours.
Before diving under the hood, pause and wonder how a bare-bones wooden cargo box bolted behind an exposed cab became America's defining machine. Born from early twentieth-century farm necessity, the pickup truck quickly escaped barnyards and conquered highways, construction sites, and suburban driveways alike.
Photo: YouTube/WD Detailing Detroit realized that utility could carry swagger, turning honest steel haulers into cultural icons that outlived chrome-drenched coupes and anchored the Motor City's bottom line for more than a century. Chevrolet joined that march in 1918 with its One-Ton Truck, followed by prewar breakthroughs like the 1929 Stovebolt inline-six and the stylish 1938 half-ton.
Postwar evolution brought the Advance Design line from 1947 to 1955 and Task Force pickups through 1959. Next came four C/K generations—1960–1966, Action Line 1967–1972, square-body Rounded Line 1973–1987, and GMT400 1988–2000—before five Silverado generations spanning GMT800, GMT900, K2XX, T1XX, and the redesigned 2027 truck.
That brings us to 1987, a pivotal swan song when General Motors renamed two-wheel-drive C-series trucks to R and four-wheel-drive K-series models to V because the incoming 1988 GMT400 debuted early in April 1987. Shortened regular-cab production totaled 269,763 Chevrolet R/V pickups: 183,857 half-ton R10 and V10 trucks, 53,522 three-quarter-ton R20 and V20 haulers, and 32,384 one-ton R30 and V30 workhorses.
Hardly exotic when new, three-quarter-ton survivors remain far scarcer than half-tons today.
Photo: YouTube/WD Detailing For 1987, Chevrolet also introduced throttle-body electronic fuel injection across its entire gasoline pickup lineup. Buyers chose between a 4.3-liter Vortec V6 with 160 hp, a 5.0-liter V8 delivering 170 hp, a 5.7-liter V8 rated at 210 hp under 8,600 pounds GVWR or 185 hp in heavy-duty trim, and a 7.4-liter big-block packing 230 hp. Diesel loyalists got a 6.2-liter V8 producing 130 hp or 148 hp in heavy-duty specification.
Transmission options spanned a 3-speed Saginaw manual, a 4-speed New Process NP833 overdrive manual, the heavy-duty 4-speed Muncie SM465 manual with a granny-low gear—the exact stick bolted inside this rescued truck—plus 3-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic 400 and 4-speed 700R4 overdrive automatics. Back in 1987, a standard two-wheel-drive R20 Fleetside long-bed started at $10,530, rising to $11,211 in upscale Silverado trim like this example, or $12,629 for the heavy-duty R20 HD Silverado.
Once the 72-hour countdown started, Adam popped the hood to grim news: no radiator, pitch-black oil, and throttle-body injection instead of a simple carburetor. The 350-cubic-inch V8 cranked with spark and barked briefly on hand-poured fuel, yet the fuel pump stayed silent. Underneath lurked a detached exhaust pipe, a rogue soup can, a missing driver-side tank, a dry rear brake reservoir, and a rusted-solid rear brake drum Adam finally hammered free before hunting parts.
Photo: YouTube/WD Detailing With 60 hours remaining, RJ Wagner attacked 15 years of barn leaves packed in the bed and revived the rust-stained white eight-lug steelies with hydrofluoric acid and iron remover. Then came a painful plot twist: a polish test turned his yellow microfiber red, confirming fragile single-stage enamel without clear coat. Chemical pre-wash was off the table, forcing slow rinsing, engine-bay degreasing, contact washes, and clay-mitting that burned the clock down to 48 hours.
Morning arrived with 36 hours left and a biohazard cabin waiting inside. RJ unbolted the rodent-trailed bucket seats, Tornador-blasted clouds of dust from the maroon carpet, evicted a mouse nest packed inside the glove box, and scrubbed sticky decades of grime off the steering wheel. Just as exhaustion peaked at 30 hours remaining, WD Garage's Mike burst in to drill-brush and extract the carpets, fragile cloth seats, and rubber GM floor mats past nightfall.
On the final morning, only 12 hours stood between triumph and an embarrassing Black Friday flop. RJ cut through chalky orange oxidation with a wool pad, resurrecting razor-sharp cherry-red reflections across the Squarebody panels. With seven hours left, Adam strolled back holding a radiator, fuel pump, injectors, and battery. Dropping the surviving passenger tank exposed a disintegrated non-fuel-rated hose and stale red gasoline, yet they bolted the rebuilt tank right back up without testing it.
Photo: YouTube/WD Detailing Sure enough, after sealing the paint and installing the radiator, turning the key with 2.5 hours left brought dead silence. Rather than dropping the tank again, Adam applied direct power, proved the pump ran, traced a broken firewall harness plug, and bypassed it to wake the pump. Still, zero fuel sprayed with one hour and 25 minutes left, until a noid light confirmed computer pulse and two fresh injectors fired the 350 to life.
With the brakes finally bled and the video due at the editor's desk ahead of its 12-hour release window, RJ slid behind the clean wheel and rolled the cherry-red 1987 Silverado 20 into the cold night. Shifting smoothly down the street and stopping on command sealed the miracle. Adam saved his paycheck, the WD Detailing crew brought home their figurative bacon, and another forgotten three-quarter-ton Squarebody proved Detroit iron never goes quietly.
